The Pyrenean brook salamander (Calotriton asper) is an endemic amphibian inhabiting cold, fast-flowing streams in the Pyrenees. At a constant water temperature of approximately 10 °C [T = 10 °C], embryonic development proceeds over 37.6 days [ab = 37.6 days], a duration that reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by the species' high-altitude environment. Upon hatching, the newly emerged larvae possess a wet weight of 0.0402 grams [Wwb = 0.0402 grams], a modest mass indicative of the small yolk reserves contained within eggs averaging 3.5 to 5.0 mm in diameter. During the larval phase, individuals grow slowly, and the transition to a post-metamorphic juvenile, marked by complete gill resorption and tail fin regression, occurs approximately 415 days after hatching  at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. At this metamorphic climax, the snout-vent length measures 1.13 centimeters , a value consistent with the conservative growth strategy observed in montane stream-dwelling urodeles.

Following metamorphosis, immature Pyrenean brook salamanders continue to accumulate body mass and skeletal length over several years before reaching reproductive maturity. For males, the onset of puberty occurs after approximately 2.75 years since birth [tp = approximately 2.75 years since birth], a developmental timeline that appears tightly linked to the attainment of a critical body size at a temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. The snout-vent length at which puberty is reached is approximately 4.8 centimeters [Lp = approximately 4.8 centimeters] for both sexes, though subtle intraspecific variation has been noted across different elevational zones within the species' range. Comparisons with other European salamandrids suggest that these maturation parameters are largely shaped by the low annual temperatures characteristic of Pyrenean headwater streams.

Adult body size in Calotriton asper displays a modest sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a slightly smaller asymptotic snout-vent length than males. The ultimate adult snout-vent length recorded in wild-caught females is 7.5 centimeters [Li = 7.5 centimeters], whereas males typically reach a final snout-vent length of 7.7 centimeters [Li = 7.7 centimeters]. This dimorphism is accompanied by corresponding differences in adult body mass. Females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 14.0 grams [Wwi = 14.0 grams], while males, which are on average both longer and more robustly built, reach an asymptotic mass of 15.2 grams [Wwi = 15.2 grams]. At the onset of puberty, individuals of both sexes weigh approximately 3.67 grams [Wwp = approximately 3.67 grams], a value that aligns closely with predictions based on the cubic relationship between linear size and volumetric body mass observed across many salamandrid genera.

Reproductive output in the Pyrenean brook salamander is constrained by both the short growing season and the low metabolic rates imposed by cold stream temperatures. This combination yields a maximum annual reproductive rate that is modest compared to lowland congeners, reflecting the energetic limitations of a cold-adapted life history. Field observations from several Pyrenean populations confirm that this low-frequency, moderate-effort reproductive strategy is consistent across the species' range, with no evidence of multiple clutches per season. The gelatinous egg masses are typically attached to the underside of submerged rocks in riffle zones, where constant water flow ensures adequate oxygenation throughout the incubation period.

Longevity data for Calotriton asper indicate that this species follows a slow-paced life history, with the maximum recorded lifespan being 26 years [am = 26 years] under natural field conditions at a mean annual temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C]. This remarkable longevity, among the highest documented for any European urodele, is thought to be an adaptive response to the unpredictability of recruitment in high-elevation stream environments. The extended adult phase allows multiple reproductive opportunities across a lifetime, partially compensating for the low annual fecundity. Regular field surveys of marked individuals in the eastern Pyrenees have confirmed that both males and females can survive for over two decades, with senescence-related declines in body condition becoming apparent only after the 20-year mark. These demographic parameters position the species as a textbook example of a slow-living, cold-adapted vertebrate with a pronounced bet-hedging reproductive strategy.
